name: 1 Corinthians
author: The letter is from Paul, with a co-worker named Sosthenes joined in the greeting. Paul was a Jew from Tarsus, in what is now southern Turkey, trained as a Pharisee (a strict teacher of Jewish law). He once persecuted Christians, but after encountering the risen Jesus he became a travelling missionary, an apostle who started churches across the Roman world. He earned his living as a tentmaker, and almost all scholars agree he wrote this letter.
audience: The first readers were the believers in Corinth, a church Paul had started around AD 50–52 during a stay of about eighteen months. Most were non-Jews, along with some Jews, and they met in one another's homes. A few years after Paul left, he heard reports of quarrels and troubles among them, and they had also written to him with questions.
era: Paul wrote around AD 53–55, most likely from the city of Ephesus, in what is now western Turkey. Corinth was a busy Roman colony in southern Greece, rebuilt by Julius Caesar in 44 BC after an earlier destruction. It sat on a narrow strip of land between two seaports, so it was crowded with traders, sailors, slaves and freed slaves, and full of temples to many gods. The Christian movement was only about twenty-five years old.

notes.1:1: Sosthenes may be the synagogue leader of that name who, according to Acts, was beaten in Corinth while Paul was there, though this is not certain.
notes.1:10: Paul had heard from members of Chloe's household that the church was splitting into groups loyal to different leaders, including Paul, Apollos and Cephas (Peter).
notes.2:1: Paul looks back to his first arrival in Corinth around AD 50, which according to Acts came straight after his visit to Athens.
notes.3:5: Apollos was an educated, eloquent Jewish Christian from Alexandria in Egypt who taught in Corinth after Paul had moved on.
notes.5:1: Paul had received a report of a church member living with his stepmother, a relationship forbidden under both Jewish and Roman law.
notes.5:9: Paul refers to an earlier letter he had written to Corinth, which has not survived.
notes.6:1: Some church members were taking one another to the city's public courts, where Roman magistrates heard civil disputes.
notes.6:12: Many scholars think Paul is quoting slogans that were popular among some Corinthian believers, then responding to them.
notes.7:1: Here Paul begins answering questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter, starting with questions about marriage.
notes.8:1: Paul answers their question about meat from animals sacrificed to idols, which was sold in markets and served at meals in temple dining rooms.
notes.9:1: Some in Corinth questioned whether Paul was a true apostle, partly because he supported himself by his trade instead of accepting payment.
notes.9:24: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, a major athletic festival where winners received a simple wreath of leaves.
notes.11:17: The Lord's Supper was then part of a shared meal in a home, and the wealthier members were apparently eating before poorer members arrived.
notes.11:23: This is the earliest written account of Jesus' Last Supper, set down before the Gospels were written.
notes.12:1: Paul turns to another question from the Corinthians' letter, this time about spiritual gifts and how they were being used in worship.
notes.15:1: Paul passes on an early summary of the faith he had received, including the oldest written list of people who saw the risen Jesus.
notes.15:12: Some in the church were saying the dead would not be raised, an idea that fit common Greek thinking, which often looked down on the body.
notes.15:29: Nobody now knows exactly what the practice of being baptised for the dead was, and scholars have offered many different explanations.
notes.16:1: Paul was organising a collection from his churches for poor believers in Jerusalem, which he planned to have delivered there.
notes.16:10: Timothy was Paul's younger co-worker, whom he had sent ahead to visit Corinth.
notes.16:19: Aquila and Priscilla, a tentmaking couple who had worked alongside Paul in Corinth, were now with him in Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia.
